title: Regularization
goal: This chapter explains when ordinary least squares becomes unreliable and how a penalty on the weights stabilizes the fit. It builds directly on the normal equations of ch01 and ends with how to choose the penalty strength honestly.

objectives.text: After this chapter you can diagnose when least squares is unreliable: more features than samples, or strongly correlated features.
After this chapter you can derive the ridge solution and explain why it exists for every \(\lambda > 0\).
After this chapter you can compare ridge and lasso and choose between them for a given goal.
After this chapter you can choose \(\lambda\) by cross-validation without leaking validation data, and explain the bias–variance trade-off it controls.

map.title: When least squares struggles
concepts: \(d > n\): the rank of \(X\) is at most \(n\), so \(X^\top X\) is singular
Correlated features: \(X^\top X\) ill-conditioned, high-variance estimates

map.title: Ridge regression
concepts: Objective \(\|y - Xw\|^2 + \lambda\|w\|^2\) and solution \((X^\top X + \lambda I)^{-1}X^\top y\)
Positive definiteness for \(\lambda > 0\); \(\lambda = 0\) recovers least squares
Standardize features, do not penalize the intercept

map.title: The lasso
concepts: \(\ell_1\) penalty, no closed form, coordinate descent

map.title: Choosing λ
concepts: Cross-validation over a grid; extend the grid when the best value is at its edge
Fit preprocessing on training folds only

quiz.prompt: Write the ridge objective and its closed-form solution.
quiz.solution: Ridge minimizes \(\|y - Xw\|^2 + \lambda\|w\|^2\) with \(\lambda > 0\). Setting the gradient to zero gives \((X^\top X + \lambda I)w = X^\top y\), so \(\hat w_{\text{ridge}} = (X^\top X + \lambda I)^{-1}X^\top y\).

quiz.prompt: Which statement about the lasso is correct?

options.text: It always keeps exactly one non-zero weight.
options.why: The number of zeros depends on \(\lambda\); it grows with \(\lambda\) but is not fixed at one survivor.

options.text: It can set some weights exactly to zero.
options.why: The absolute-value penalty produces exact zeros, which is why the lasso performs feature selection.

options.text: Its solution is \((X^\top X + \lambda I)^{-1}X^\top y\).
options.why: That is the ridge solution; the lasso has no closed form in general.
\(\lambda\) still has to be chosen, typically by cross-validation.

quiz.solution: Only B holds. The \(\ell_1\) penalty is not differentiable at zero, and that kink is what lets some weights land exactly on zero as \(\lambda\) grows.

quiz.prompt: Explain why the least-squares closed form of ch01 cannot be used with 40 samples and 60 features.
quiz.solution: The closed form needs \(X^\top X\) to be invertible, which requires linearly independent columns (ch01, §1.3). With 60 features and 40 samples the rank of \(X\) is at most 40, so the 60 × 60 matrix \(X^\top X\) has rank at most 40 and is singular.

quiz.prompt: Use the data of ch01 (Q3): \(X = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 0\\ 1 & 1\\ 1 & 2\end{pmatrix}\), \(y = (1, 2, 4)^\top\). With \(\lambda = 1\), and penalizing both weights for this exercise only, compute the ridge estimate and compare it with the least-squares one.
quiz.solution:
\(X^\top X + I = \begin{pmatrix}4 & 3\\ 3 & 6\end{pmatrix}\), determinant \(24 - 9 = 15\), \(X^\top y = (7, 10)^\top\).

\(\hat w_{\text{ridge}} = \tfrac{1}{15}\begin{pmatrix}6 & -3\\ -3 & 4\end{pmatrix}(7, 10)^\top = (12/15,\ 19/15)^\top \approx (0.800, 1.267)\).

The least-squares estimate was \(\approx (0.833, 1.5)\): both weights shrink toward zero, the slope more.

quiz.prompt: "Choosing \(\lambda\) as the value with the lowest training error is a sound strategy."
quiz.solution: False. Training error only grows as \(\lambda\) increases, so this rule would always pick the smallest \(\lambda\) — plain least squares — and ignore variance entirely. \(\lambda\) must be chosen on held-out data, by cross-validation.

quiz.prompt: A pipeline standardizes all the data, then runs 5-fold cross-validation over \(\lambda \in \{0.01, 0.1, 1\}\), and the best value is 1. Identify two problems and how to fix them.
quiz.solution: First, standardizing all the data before splitting leaks the validation folds' means and standard deviations into training; the standardization must be fitted inside each training fold. Second, the best value sits at the edge of the grid, so the true optimum may be larger: extend the grid and search again.

readings.citation: Hoerl, A. E., & Kennard, R. W. (1970). Ridge Regression: Biased Estimation for Nonorthogonal Problems. *Technometrics*, 12(1), 55–67.
readings.adds: The original paper behind §2.2. It motivates ridge with strongly correlated predictors, shows that some positive \(\lambda\) gives a lower mean squared error than least squares, and introduces the ridge trace — the plot of coefficients against \(\lambda\) that exercise 2.2 asks you to draw.

readings.citation: Tibshirani, R. (1996). Regression Shrinkage and Selection via the Lasso. *Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series B*, 58(1), 267–288.
readings.adds: The paper that introduced the lasso of §2.3. It frames the penalty as a constraint on the sum of absolute coefficients, explains geometrically why that constraint produces exact zeros, and positions the method between subset selection and ridge.
